items.title: Bas-Mono/Aménagement des pistes rurales: Des populations riveraines sensibilisées sur le plan d’action de réinstallation
items.description: Afagnan, 6 nov. (ATOP) – Une équipe du ministère en charge des Pistes rurales a sensibilisé les populations et chefs des services déconcentrés de l’état sur le Plan d’action de réinstallation et de réinsertion (PARR) des personnes lors d’une tournée d’informations, effectuée du 4 au 6 novembre à Afagnan. Cette démarche s’inscrit dans le cadre du projet de réhabilitation et de réaménagement des pistes rurales au Togo. Ledit projet est porté par le gouvernement à travers le ministère en charge des Pistes rurales. Il bénéficie du soutien technique et financier volontaire de la banque allemande de développement (KFW) et de l’Agence français de développement (AFD). L’ambition est de réaménager au moins 1000 km sur toute l’étendue du territoire national. Les assises ont permis d’informer les populations sur les objectifs du projet et son principe, le mode de mise en œuvre du PARR des personnes affectées par le projet. Il s’agit aussi de recueillir les préoccupations, les suggestions, les avis, et les doléances des populations. Les échanges ont porté sur le recensement des biens dans les emprises, la prise en compte des personnes affectées notamment le système de donation volontaire pour les biens mineurs qui seront impactés dans les emprises. Les discussions ont, aussi, axé sur la protection de l’environnement, les risques d’accidents, de violences basées sur le genre, les impacts négatifs, la pollution de l’environnement et les comportements à adopter pendant les travaux. Le chef de l’équipe, Akakpo Kokouda, consultant sur l’aspect social pour la réalisation des travaux, a invité les populations à s’impliquer pleinement pour la réussite du projet. Selon lui, ce projet vise à désenclaver les localités, à faciliter l’écoulement des produits agricoles et à améliorer l’accès des populations aux soins sociaux de base. Il a indiqué que dans les agglomérations, les pistes vont mesurer 8 m et 12 m dans les campagnes. Dans la préfecture de Bas-Mono, cinq pistes sont concernées à savoir, les pistes reliant (Anfoin-Attitogon-Afagnan), (Tokplie-Agomé-Glozou), (Afagnan Gbleta-Kpetsou-Dzrekpo Hagou), (Afagnagan- Logowomé-Masseda) et (klologo-Momé Gbavé-Afagnan). Sur ces axes, il est prévu des travaux d’ouverture, de reprofilage, de chargement systématique de gravier, de construction d’ouvrage de franchissement et d’entretien courant. ATOP/DK/DHK

items.title: CRIEF : Général Mathurin Bangoura et ses co-prévenus attendus le 16 décembre prochain
items.description: Sauf changement de dernière minute, les débats dans le procès opposant le parquet spécial à l’ancien gouverneur de la ville de Conakry, le général Mathurin Bangoura et ses co-prévenus devraient s’ouvrir le mercredi 16 décembre 2026. Cette décision émane de la chambre de jugement de la Cour de répression des infractions économiques et financières (CRIEF), présidée par Alpha Camara. Les prévenus, Mathurin Bangoura, Mori Diané et la Société guinéenne des mines SA, sont poursuivis à la suite d’une plainte de la société Réma Tip Top Guinea SARL. Ils répondent de faits présumés d’escroquerie, d’abus de confiance, de faux et usage de faux en écriture authentique et de commerce, ainsi que d’entrave aux droits d’un actionnaire de participer à une assemblée générale. Lors de l’audience du 4 novembre dernier, les prévenus ont brillé par leur absence. Face à cette situation, la cour a renvoyé l’affaire au 16 décembre prochain pour leur comparution. Il convient de préciser qu’une seconde procédure opposant les deux parties est également pendante devant la même juridiction. Dans ce volet, le général Mathurin Bangoura, Mori Diané et la Société guinéenne des mines SA poursuivent à leur tour la société Réma Tip Top Guinée SA, ainsi qu’Alpha Oumar Bah et Abdoulaye Barry, pour des faits présumés d’escroquerie et de complicité d’escroquerie. Cette seconde affaire a également été renvoyée au 16 décembre prochain pour la comparution des prévenus. items.title: Hockey Finally Has the Great Books It Deserves
items.description: Pity the Canadian book reviewer in the autumn of 1980. An American publisher has announced, with some fanfare, a forthcoming title about the national pastime—the Canadian national pastime. Amazons: An Intimate Memoir by the First Woman Ever to Play in the National Hockey League promises to tell the story of Cleo Birdwell’s debut season with the New York Rangers. Of course, as a Canadian in good standing, you know that no woman has ever played in the NHL; there is no Cleo Birdwell. But the people behind the book are committed to the bit. At the Canadian Booksellers Association convention, held that summer in Toronto, a leggy model impersonated Birdwell, signing advance copies in a Rangers jersey. “She’s tough and sexy,” the book’s publisher whispered to a Globe and Mail reporter. Clearly this book demands attention. Perhaps the charade might even provide a welcome distraction after Canada’s rather unmiraculous sixth-place finish at Lake Placid. But what awaits within its pages confounds. The on-ice action is overshadowed by ever more elaborate accounts of Birdwell’s sexual adventures. In the course of one season, she sleeps with the Rangers’ head coach, the Rangers’ general manager, a former Rangers player, and one very jet-lagged tennis star. This is an incomplete list. In the brutal assessment of one critic in Calgary, Amazons is “little more than hardcover softcore porn that will disappoint hockey fans and heavy breathers alike.” But Amazons wasn’t smut, or not exactly. Its author was Don DeLillo. His publisher took pains to guard this secret, but there was no disguising his writing from those who already admired it. Colin McEnroe , reviewing the book for the Hartford Courant , seems to have been the first to identify DeLillo’s authorship in print. “ ‘Amazons’ is not only his book,” he wrote. “It’s his best book.” DeLillo did not share this appraisal. Although the book sold well—better, in fact, than any of his previous novels—he would not allow it to be republished. Even after the breakout success of White Noise in 1985, it never appeared in his official bibliography. Amazons soon faded into obscurity. I first learned of its existence in 2006, when the writer Keith Gessen published an essay in The New York Times Book Review titled “ In Search of the Great American Hockey Novel .” Gessen wrote of his dismay that hockey had not produced a literature as rich as that of boxing or baseball. “Where is the Chekhov of the Chicago Blackhawks?” he asked. “Who is the Stendhal of the stick to the groin?” On the shelf dedicated to immortal hockey books, Gessen placed just two volumes: Ken Dryden’s melancholy 1983 memoir, The Game , about his final season with the dynastic Montreal Canadiens, and DeLillo’s Amazons . Hockey and literature were two pursuits struggling to find an audience; perhaps, Gessen ventured, they could help each other. “What is needed now, for the sake of both hockey and literature, is more hockey literature,” he wrote. “Not just books about hockey, like ‘The Game,’ but also books not about hockey, like ‘Amazons’—which is not about hockey in just the right way.” Gessen may have been only half serious, but two decades after his essay appeared, something like his modest proposal has come to pass. The Intangibles , a new memoir by the New Yorker staff writer Nick Paumgarten, is a worthy successor to The Game , no less so for describing a career played in bruising beer leagues. The success of Heated Rivalry on HBO Max has made Rachel Reid’s queer-romance series, from which it was adapted, into a publishing juggernaut. Hockey erotica, once a fringe category, has become a cottage industry. Following that unlikely turn of events—and a January story in the Times positing DeLillo as the genre’s unlikely inventor—his editor and agent entreated him to allow Amazons back into print. DeLillo acquiesced. After 46 years, Cleo Birdwell is finally making her curtain call. A mazons was not DeLillo’s first foray into the world of sport. That distinction belongs to End Zone , his heady 1972 novel about college football and the madness of mutual assured destruction. Later, in the prologue to Underworld (1997), he turned to baseball, with his panoramic account of Bobby Thomson’s “shot heard ’round the world.” In those pages, too, nuclear war hangs in the air; the White House announced on the same day in 1951 that the Soviet Union had conducted a bomb test. The tone of Amazons is zanier, more absurd, untroubled by nuclear annihilation. If anything hangs in the air, it’s the reek of the hockey bag. Cleo Birdwell is the pride of Badger, Ohio, which she describes as a small, straightforward town where “the school was on School Street, the bank was on Bank Street, the river ran by River Road.” But Cleo is not an ingenue; she’s a hockey player. No amount of towel snapping or jock talk seems capable of making her blush. On the contrary, she’s a wry raconteur of her teammates’ puerile antics. One player, Eric Torkleson, has such an enormous member that it becomes an honorary Ranger, known as Torkle. “A player would say, ‘How’s Torkle doing today?’ Or, ‘Who’s playing Torkle in the movie version?’ Or, ‘Is it true Torkle’s being asked to endorse Jimmy Carter?’ ” The book is as sex-drenched as the Calgary reviewer warned. But sex functions less as titillation and more as the engine of the satire. Its object, mostly, is the American male. Cleo is frank, confident, liberated; her lovers are neurotic and narcissistic. One, the Rangers’ general manager, is unable to perform after Cleo makes an offhanded Watergate joke. How could he, having been reminded of this great blow to the male ego? “We lost our manhood, our sense of pride and honor, our belief in God and Dick Nixon, our deepest dreams, hopes, and ambitions.” (In an earlier scene, the GM has been deflated by intrusive thoughts of Torkle.) Men who aren’t trying to sleep with Cleo are usually trying to persuade her to sell something—the rank commercialization of sport is one of the novel’s many prescient targets. Cleo is asked to hawk a sensual whirlpool bath called the Primal Vortex and a snack food called Amazons, especially formulated for “every age, every size, every make of woman.” She refuses both endorsements. In the middle of the Rangers’ season, Hughes Tool, the conglomerate that owns the team, hires a Saudi national to run it, hoping to push through a business deal with “men in the Gulf.” DeLillo seems to have anticipated our age of sportswashing, too. To be clear, Amazons is not a lost masterpiece. Some scenes drag, like runaway SNL sketches. The dialogue, although generally hilarious, can take on a rim-shot quality, as if DeLillo were doing Dangerfield. A sportswriter confesses to Cleo that his ex-wife is now a lesbian. “Who is she a lesbian with?” she asks. “Paine, Webber, Jackson and Curtis. She’s a financial analyst.” Robert Gottlieb, DeLillo’s editor at the time, turned down Amazons . You wonder how the man who convinced Joseph Heller that Catch‑22 sounded funnier than Catch‑18 might have sharpened this manuscript. [ From the May 1973 issue: “The Bucky Wunderlick Story,” by Don DeLillo ] As for the hockey quotient, some fans may wish that DeLillo had set more of the novel between the boards. But Amazons is like Dickie Dunn’s newspaper accounts of the Charlestown Chiefs in Slap Shot : It captures the spirit of the thing. The locker-room banter, at once clever and cretinous; the relentless travel to frozen, past-their-prime cities; the vicious play of the Philadelphia Flyers and the bloodlust of their fans (“screaming made-up and never-before-heard obscenities, as though they were overwhelmed by a massive thyroid deficiency”); the otherworldly allure of a sport conducted, improbably, on a sheet of ice. “In a way it is the most romantic game,” the Rangers’ head coach, Jean-Paul Larousse, says. “There is a lightness, a speed without effort. It is the skates.” It was lightness and speed that drew Nick Paumgarten to hockey. On land, he was ungainly: “You run like a goof,” his brother once told him. “But on the ice the hobbles fell away. With skates on my feet, I could glide, swerve, cut, and feel for a few seconds at least that I’d broken the code, whatever it was.” Paumgarten grew up playing hockey in New York City. His junior career petered out in prep school, but for much of his adult life, he’s competed in Manhattan’s beer leagues. He’s played on ragtag teams with only-in–New York linemates: creative types, a master crane rigger, a guy who used to be Woody Allen’s super. Some are ringers fresh out of college; others are graybeards holding on for one more season of glory. Not that there is much glory to be had when the puck drops at 11:30 p.m. on the far west side. “We did it for no one but ourselves, and really it was more like we were doing it to ourselves,” he writes in The Intangibles . “It was more destructive than constructive: murderous to our daylight ambitions and obligations, hard on the joints, and maybe equally hard on our families and friends.” So why do it? For fellowship, for laughs, for escape, for the spirit of the thing. To find what hockey players call the absolute beauties, like-minded men who play the right way: “with a commitment not just to proper comportment and teamwork but also to sticking around for postgame beers and high- and low-minded banter. A sense of humor, a sense of absurdity.” The Intangibles, the team that gives the memoir its name, plays the right way. It has some elite skaters but also plenty of grinders, the guys you can count on to show up, hustle, and, if necessary, intimidate the opposition, like the maniacal Flyers of old. The license to exact a measure of retribution for a cheap shot or a high stick, for running up the score or running your mouth—this, too, is part of hockey’s ethos, and its appeal to men arriving at the rink from jobs, white collar or blue, that may offer fewer opportunities to administer just deserts. Paumgarten himself is not above such belligerent displays. “On the ice,” he writes, “in this realm circumscribed by boards and Plexiglas and patrolled by men in stripes, an artificial universe where you dart around in a suit of armor, with wings on your feet and levers in your hands, it is a privilege and a joy to shove and slash and tell people to fuck off, to be a jerk to strangers, without it being in any way an actionable affront.” Someone tell Keith Gessen: We have found the Stendhal of the stick to the groin. Though I suspect he already knows this. One of the Intangibles is a writer, referred to only as Keith, who often composes arch postgame emails, recording for posterity the team’s triumphs and follies. I’m pretty sure I recognize the voice. This article appears in the December 2026 print edition with the headline “An Absolute Beauty.”

items.title: Manganèse : un investissement de 116,7 milliards de FCFA annoncé à M’Bembélé
items.description: Le Gabon franchit une nouvelle étape dans son ambition de transformation locale du manganèse. Un mémorandum d’entente a été signé, le 6 novembre en Chine, avec South Manganese Investment Limited pour développer un complexe métallurgique à M’Bembélé, dans la région de Ndjolé. L’investissement est estimé à 116,7 milliards de FCFA. Emmanuel Eyeghe Nze, le 6 novembre 2026 à Pékin, après la signature d’un mémorandum d’entente avec Zhang He, PCA de South Manganese Investment Limited. © D.R. Le projet de transformation industrielle du manganèse gabonais prend progressivement forme. Le ministre du Commerce, de l’Industrie et de la Transformation, Emmanuel Eyeghe Nze, a annoncé, le 6 novembre 2026, la signature d’un mémorandum d’entente avec Zhang He, président du conseil d’administration de South Manganese Investment Limited. L’accord porte sur le développement d’un projet intégré de transformation locale du minerai extrait à M’Bembélé, dans la région de Ndjolé. Estimé à 116,7 milliards de FCFA, cet investissement matérialise les intentions précédemment exprimées par les responsables de CICMHZ, filiale gabonaise du groupe chinois, reçus en audience par les autorités gabonaises. Pour Libreville, cette signature marque le passage des annonces à une perspective concrète d’investissement industriel. Plus d’un million de tonnes à l’horizon 2030 Dans sa première phase, le projet prévoit une capacité de production annuelle de 180 000 tonnes de produits métallurgiques. Celle-ci devrait ensuite connaître une progression graduelle pour dépasser le million de tonnes par an à l’horizon 2030. Au-delà des capacités industrielles annoncées, les retombées attendues concernent également la création d’emplois, le transfert de compétences et le développement de nouvelles filières économiques. Autant de leviers susceptibles de renforcer la valeur ajoutée générée localement par l’exploitation du manganèse. Le cap de la transformation locale maintenu Cette initiative s’inscrit dans la stratégie gouvernementale visant à réduire progressivement l’exportation des matières premières à l’état brut. «Faire du Gabon un pays qui ne se contente plus d’extraire et d’exporter ses ressources naturelles, mais qui les transforme davantage sur son propre territoire» , a rappelé Emmanuel Eyeghe Nze. Portée par le président Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema, cette orientation fixe notamment à 2029 un cap pour la transformation locale des ressources stratégiques, dont le manganèse. Reste désormais à traduire les engagements du mémorandum en réalisations industrielles. Pour le Gabon, qui ambitionne de consolider sa base productive, le développement de M’Bembélé constitue un nouveau test de sa capacité à convertir son potentiel minier en richesse créée sur le territoire national. items.title: Manéah : des travailleurs de Topaz manifestent pour réclamer deux mois de salaires impayés
items.description: La colère est montée d’un cran dans la matinée de ce vendredi à Manéah, où plus de 2 500 travailleurs de la société Topaz ont manifesté dans l’enceinte de leur entreprise pour réclamer le paiement de deux mois d’arriérés de salaires. Mis en congé technique depuis deux mois, à la suite de la décision du gouvernement de suspendre la production des sachets en plastiques, ces employés dénoncent une situation devenue de plus en plus difficile pour eux et leurs familles. Munis de pancartes et scandant des slogans réclamant le paiement immédiat de leurs droits, les manifestants ont bloqué l’entrée de l’entreprise afin de faire entendre leurs revendications. À travers cette mobilisation, ils entendent interpeller aussi bien les autorités que la direction de Topaz sur leurs conditions de vie, fortement affectées par cette période prolongée sans rémunération. « Nous sommes en congé technique depuis deux mois, mais jusqu’à présent, nous n’avons reçu aucun salaire. Nous avons des familles à nourrir, des loyers à payer et des enfants à scolariser. Nous demandons simplement le paiement de nos deux mois d’arriérés. Nous ne réclamons rien d’autre que nos droits », a confié Mohamed, l’un des manifestants. Un autre travailleur, visiblement préoccupé par la situation, interpelle directement les autorités : « cette décision a plongé des milliers de travailleurs dans une situation très difficile. Nous comprenons les mesures prises par le gouvernement, mais nous ne devons pas être abandonnés. Nous demandons aux autorités et aux responsables de l’entreprise de trouver rapidement une solution pour nous permettre de rentrer en possession de nos salaires. » Face à cette mobilisation, les responsables communaux de Manéah ont reçu une délégation des manifestants. Les échanges ont permis de calmer les esprits. Les autorités communales ont, à cette occasion, promis de s'impliquer afin de contribuer à trouver une issue favorable à la situation dans les meilleurs délais. En attendant des mesures concrètes, les travailleurs de Topaz restent dans l'expectative. Au-delà de leurs revendications salariales, cette situation met en lumière les conséquences sociales de l'arrêt de la production des sachets plastiques, qui fragilise des milliers de travailleurs et leurs familles.

items.title: Tour du Faso 2026: Paul Daumont prend le maillot jaune à la 8e étape
items.description: Le cycliste burkinabè Paul Daumont a pris, ce vendredi 6 novembre 2026, le maillot jaune, à l’issue de la course de la 8 e étape de la 37 e édition du Tour du Faso, courue entre Ouagadougou-Koupela. La 8 e édition du Tour du Faso a été courue, ce vendredi 6 novembre 2026, entre Ouagadougou et Koupela sur une distance de 153,05 km, repartie en 3 sprints intermédiaires. Au total, ce sont 69 coureurs qui étaient au départ de cette étape. Le premier point chaud à Koulbila (60,57 Km) a été remporté par l’Algérien Anes Riahi qui a été suivi par le Marocain Youssef Bdadou (2 e ) et le Sud Africain Emile Van Nierkerk arrivé 3 e . Le 2 e point chaud à Mogtedo d’une distance de 98,51 Km a vu Riahi franchir en premier la ligne, en 2 e position Bdadou et la 3 e place est occupée par Jannes Van Weele des Pays Bas. L’Algérien Anes Riahi vient encore en première position au 3e point chaud à Zorgho, long de 122,01 Km. Il est toujours suivi par Youssef Bdadou et le Burkinabè Paul Daumont en 3 e position. Cette 8 e étape a été remportée par l’Algérien Anes Riahi. Quant au maillot jaune, il est désormais sur les épaules du Burkinabè Paul Daumont qui a terminé la course troisième qui était détenu par le Sud-Africain Gustav Basson. L’étape a enregistré un abandon. Il s’agit de l’Algérien Hamza Yacine qui a remporté trois étapes du Tour. Il a été victime d’une chute hier à Pô. Par Wakat Séra L’article Tour du Faso 2026: Paul Daumont prend le maillot jaune à la 8e étape est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: How China's clean-tech machine is reshaping the global climate fight
items.description: China sent $132 billion in clean technology and investment to the developing world last year, by far the largest contribution to carbon-dioxide reduction of any country. In fact, the nation’s green-manufacturing juggernaut, built in part through heavy subsidies from Beijing, nearly matches the current total of grants, loans and private finance that all wealthy countries sent to poorer ones in 2024 to help fight climate change, according to a Reuters analysis. Those loans and grants stemmed from a climate-finance programme the world’s wealthiest nations agreed to at a 2009 United Nations climate conference on the premise that industrialised nations made outsized contributions to the climate crisis — and had outsized means to help poorer countries pay to clean it up. A Reuters investigation in 2024 found that most global climate finance comes in the form of loans and sometimes at market interest rates that funnel billions of dollars back to rich countries. China took a different approach, funneling billions in subsidies into its own green-energy industries , serving its own national interest to dominate next-generation manufacturing domestically and globally. The result: massive and rapid market-share gains in solar panels, batteries and battery minerals, electric vehicles, wind turbines and other green products. China remains by far the world’s biggest greenhouse-gas emitter because of its large population, concentration of heavy industry and reliance on coal power. But its huge clean tech exports mean it has also become among the biggest global forces in reducing climate-damaging emissions. The Reuters analysis used customs data to calculate the value of Chinese exports of clean technologies to countries classified by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development as developing nations. Those exports alone will help the Global South avoid 257 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions (MtCO2) per year once deployed an amount equal to the annual carbon dioxide emissions of France, according to analysis by Lauri Myllyvirta, co-founder of the Helsinki-based Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air. This year’s exports from China, meanwhile, are on track to avoid 337 MtCO2 in the Global South, the analysis shows. Reuters was unable to find a reliable single estimate of how much greenhouse gas emissions are avoided as a result of global climate finance from rich to poor countries. The OECD estimates a fifth of all rich world climate giving in 2024 came from the private sector. The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change and the High Ambition Coalition — an informal coalition of nations that has advocated for substantial climate finance — did not immediately comment for this story. The $132bn figure derived by Reuters for China’s global climate contribution also includes an estimated $40 billion of Chinese foreign direct investment into clean-technology projects in developing countries. The investment data was compiled by Mathias Larsen and Xiaokang Xue at the London School of Economics. That brings China’s contribution to nearly equal to the $137bn in climate finance that wealthy nations provided to poorer ones in 2024 under their UN climate pledges, according to the most recent figures provided by the OECD. The figures are not directly comparable. China’s total largely reflects commercial transactions focused on clean energy development, while climate finance can also support other types of programs like developing climate-resilient agricultural techniques or cleaning up damage from major storms or floods. But the comparison illustrates the extraordinary scale at which China’s manufacturing economy is now shaping the energy transition in poorer countries. The findings point to a potential shift in the mechanics of the global energy transition, according to Li Shuo, a veteran observer of China at UN climate talks who heads the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute. For years, climate talks focused on how much money and technology wealthy countries would provide to poorer ones to help them decarbonise. China’s manufacturing boom is creating another pathway: driving down the price of clean technology through self-interested innovation and scale until developing countries adopt it for economic reasons. “You can align it to your economic agenda,” he said. Export giant, diplomatic mouse Beijing has so far shown little interest in translating its commercial might into diplomatic leadership at global climate talks since President Donald Trump withdrew the United States from international climate cooperation in 2025. China’s diplomatic role likely will take centre stage as nations gather this month for the UN’s COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Turkiye. Bilateral agreements between heavyweights Washington and Beijing have traditionally paved the way for international climate agreements, including the landmark 2015 Paris deal to limit global warming. But Beijing may be unwilling to go on alone without its geopolitical counterweight at the table, according to former climate negotiators. Beijing may also be worried that taking a bold stance on global carbon reduction would bring unwanted pressure for China to give more climate aid or cut its own fossil-fuel emissions, observers say. China emits about a third of all carbon dioxide emissions and still burns coal for more than half its power. “How China engages on different levels in the coming years is the most fundamental thing that is going to happen on climate because of both their role in clean-tech deployment but also because of their emissions profile,” said Jennifer Morgan, Germany’s former climate minister. China’s Ministry of Commerce said the country is an important contributor to the global green transformation, and that its wind and solar exports have cumulatively reduced global emissions by roughly 4.1bn tonnes of CO2 over the past five years — the equivalent of around 80 per cent of the total emissions of the United States in one year. “Against the backdrop of a global climate governance ‘action deficit’, China will continue to uphold a responsible attitude, working with other countries to address challenges, overcome difficulties, and jointly promote global green and low-carbon transformation and sustainable development,” it said. Forcing out fossil fuels Meanwhile, China’s manufacturing boom has made renewable energy more affordable in the developing world. When Ethiopia banned combustion engine car imports in 2024, for example, it was the first country to take such a dramatic step toward electric vehicles. The decision was less about emissions and more about cutting its fuel import bill, its deputy minister of transport at the time told Reuters . “No one in Ethiopia is asking COP to pay for any of this; the economics have just switched. It is just the cheapest and best solution,” said Larsen, a senior policy fellow at the London School of Economics, who built the database of Chinese green investment used by Reuters in this story. China has been by far the world’s biggest supplier of electric vehicles over the past few years, as dozens of subsidised automakers have waged a fierce price war in China and dramatically increased exports. The green transition has been similarly pragmatic in Pakistan , which imported 17GW worth of solar from China last year, according to data from Ember, roughly on par with Germany’s installations that year. Those panels will cut emissions and, more importantly, provide cheap, reliable power in a country that often has neither. Nearly two thirds of China’s exports of solar panels, and the cells needed to make them, went to the developing world last year, according to Reuters analysis of customs data. The picture is different in wealthy countries like the US and parts of Europe, which in recent years have imposed tariffs and other restrictions on Chinese clean technology to protect their domestic manufacturers from the surge in shipments. The US, for example, imposes tariffs exceeding 100pc on Chinese electric vehicles and has taken other measures to effectively block them from the market. “What is striking is that policies originally designed to address climate change are now facing opposition not because of their climate impacts, but because of concerns about trade and competitiveness,” said Andr Corra do Lago, a veteran climate negotiator for Brazil, which hosted last years climate summit.

items.title: 37e Tour du Faso/8e étape : Paul Daumont s’empare du maillot jaune à Koupèla
items.description: L'Algérien Anes Riahi a remporté la 8e étape du 37e Tour du Faso courue entre Ouagadougou et Koupèla le vendredi 6 novembre 2026. Longue de 152,64 km la distance a été couverte en 3h23'54 » avec une vitesse moyenne de 44,916 km/h. Paul Daumont du Burkina Faso, 3e à l'arrivée s’empare du maillot jaune de leader. Très attendu, Paul Daumont, vainqueur de l'édition 2025 remet la main sur la tunique de leader à deux étapes du terme. Le Burkinabè parti dans une échappée avec trois autres coureurs à une trentaine de km de l'arrivée a réussi à déjoué la vigilance du porteur du maillot jaune pour la lui arracher à Koupèla grâce à sa 3e place sur le podium du jour. La victoire est revenue à l'Algérien Anes Riahi qui signe le 5e succès d'étape de l'Algérie. Le Marocain Youssef Bdadou est arrivé (2e). Après l'abandon de Yacine Hamza pour cause de blessure, ils étaient 69 au départ de cette 8e étape. Le premier point chaud à Koulbila a été enlevé par l'Algérien Anes Riahi suivi du Marocain Youssef Bdadou et de Emile Van Niekerk de l'Afrique du Sud. Le cycliste algérien va comme la veille s'adjuger les deux autres sprints intermédiaires à Mogtédo puis à Zogho avant de s'imposer sur la ligne finale. Au classement général, hormis le jaune, le maillot vert change d'épaules et est désormais porté par Youssef Bdadou qui garde le maillot des points chauds. Le Burkinabè Soumaïla Ilboudo conserve la tunique du meilleur jeune. Voro KORAHIRE

items.description: Click to expand Image Palais des Nations in Geneva, Switzerland, June 16, 2025. © 2025 Lian Yi/Xinhua via Getty Images The United States is scheduled to appear in Geneva on November 10 for its Universal Periodic Review, the United Nations’ peer review process of every member state’s rights record. But the US is unlikely to show: the Trump administration declared in 2025 that the US would not participate. After the US failed to turn up in November 2025, the review was rescheduled. Should the US again fail to appear next week, it should not be given another extension and should not be exempt from this process which, as the name suggests, applies to every UN member country. As part of the process, US and international rights groups, including Human Rights Watch, made 192 submissions highlighting a range of human rights issues. The civil society submissions paint a worrying picture, with a dramatic worsening of the US government’s rights record over the past year. At President Trump’s direction, the US government dismantled its civil rights enforcement apparatus. It has also violated the prohibition on non-refoulement and sent Venezuelan men to torture in El Salvador’s prisons. The Trump administration also continues to retaliate against opponents, restrict the rights of transgender people, and eliminate regulations that curb climate warming pollutants, among other things. In an unprecedented assault on the rule of law, the administration escalated its sanctions against the ICC, targeting the court as a whole. State legislation and targeted federal funding cuts have dramatically reduced access to safe abortion care and other reproductive health care in many states, curtailing women’s rights. During the immigration crackdown, authorities have separated breastfeeding and other parents from their children and have detained pregnant women despite a longstanding government policy that directs agencies to avoid this except in limited circumstances. The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights has highlighted concerns about deaths in immigration detention; harmful migration policies and enforcement; and sanctions against the ICC and Palestinian rights groups. The UN Special Procedures mandate holders have also raised concerns regarding: unlawful killings at sea; allegedly arbitrary removal of immigration judges and politicization of immigration courts; and unlawful use of lethal force by immigration enforcement agents. The US government is attempting to dodge international scrutiny of these serious and well-documented abuses. The Human Rights Council should not let that happen. This is a time for greater rights scrutiny in the US, not less.

items.title: Imaan, Hadi move IHC against conviction in security breach case
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Human rights lawyer Imaan Zainab Mazari-Hazir and her spouse Hadi Ali Chattha on Friday filed appeals in the Islamabad High Court (IHC) against their convictions by an anti-terrorism court in the security breach case. They also moved applications seeking the suspension of their sentences and release on bail pending appeal. The appeals were filed by advocates Faisal Siddiqui, Riasat Ali Azad and Zainab Janjua under Section 25 of the Anti-Terrorism Act read with Section 410 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) against the court’s order. On Oct 29, an ATC sentenced Imaan and Hadi to 10 years in prison each in the security breach case. The court also handed down one-year sentences and imposed fines of Rs50,000 each under Section 186 (obstructing a public servant in the discharge of public functions) of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC). They were also sentenced to two years each under Section 353 (assault or criminal force to deter a public servant from discharging his duty) of the PPC. In the identical appeals, the counsel contended that the trial court failed to meet the requirements of a fair trial and that the conviction was the result of patently illegal and arbitrary proceedings. It was argued that the charge was framed without providing copies under Section 265-C CrPC and that a plea of “not guilty” was recorded on the appellants’ behalf although none was taken. They further submitted that the prosecution evidence was recorded in the absence of the appellants and their counsel, contrary to Section 353 CrPC and Article 10-A of the Constitution. The appeal also challenged the jail trial, arguing that it was conducted in a manner akin to a secret trial and without lawful authority, and that the appellants were not allowed a proper and confidential consultation with their counsel. It further contended that state counsel was imposed on the appellants against their stated wishes and that the trial court proceeded with the case despite a transfer application pending before the high court, in violation of Section 526(8) of the CrPC. On the merits, the appeal argued that the conviction under Section 7 of the ATA was unsustainable because the prosecution failed to prove the design or purpose required under Section 6 of the ATA. It said the trial court itself described the incident as “a very common nature, ordinary type of incident” and that the evidence showed the appellants were on their way to court when they were held up at the barrier. The appellants have prayed that the impugned judgment be set aside and that they be acquitted. Meanwhile, in the accompanying suspension applications, their counsel sought suspension of the sentences and release on bail, contending that the conviction was rendered during the pendency of a transfer application and that the bar under Section 25(8) of the ATA was not absolute when read with Section 25(5) of the law. ‘Misuse of criminal justice system’ Separately, over 20 international human rights organisations, including Amnesty International, called on the government to “immediately and unconditionally” release Imaan and Hadi. In a joint statement on Friday, 23 organisations, including Alliance for Lawyers at Risk, Défense Sans Frontière, New York City Bar Association, Council of Bars and Law Societies of Europe, Geneva Bar Association, Lawyers for Lawyers, and PEN Norway, condemned the recent sentences and sought an end to the “extensive misuse” of the criminal justice system against the two lawyers. It said that the convictions raised serious concerns over anti-terrorism legislation being used “to criminally punish and intimidate lawyers undertaking permissible human rights work”. Referring to the case proceedings, the statement noted that the verdict was delivered despite a petition pending in the Supreme Court. “Proceedings in these circumstances raise concerns about respect for due process and the right to an effective judicial remedy,” the organisations said, expressing concern that the trial, which was conducted at the Adiala jail in Rawalpindi, did not meet fair trial standards. The organisations noted that the couple had been kept in a “cage-like” structure in the courtroom throughout the trial, rendering them unable to communicate with their counsel effectively. They also noted that the counsel was not given sufficient access to Imaan and Hadi. “The prosecution relied primarily on police testimony to establish the offence, while the defence were denied adequate opportunity to reasonably challenge prosecutorial evidence,” the statement read, adding that the couple had denied the charges and maintained they were being targeted for their professional work and activism. The organisations raised alarm that the “misuse of overbroad anti-terrorism legislation to the alleged removal of security barriers raises serious questions about the proportionality of the charges”. It observed that such legislation must not be applied “arbitrarily or disproportionately, nor used to intimidate individuals or punish permissible conduct or activities that do not meet the applicable threshold”. The organisations called for the convictions to be seen in the context of “successive, politically motivated, criminal proceedings” against the couple, which were “solely to punish them for and deter them from continuing their peaceful, permissible human rights work”. They also recalled the SC’s September 17 suspension of their 17-year sentences in the social media posts case and subsequent rearrest. “The successive proceedings in the barrier removal case, and their prolonged deprivation of liberty despite the SC’s intervention, reinforce our concern that the criminal proceedings are calculated to make an example of the two lawyers and risk creating a chilling effect on the independence of the legal profession in Pakistan and on access to justice more broadly.” In this regard, the organisations cited Article 10A of the Constitution, which guarantees the right to a fair trial and due process, as well as Pakistan’s status as a party to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR). “Anti-terrorism legislation must not be used to criminalise peaceful assembly, protected expression, freedom of association or permissible professional activity,” the organisations stated. “The arrest, prosecution or prolonged detention of the lawyers because of their professional representation, human rights advocacy and exercise of their right to freedom of expression not only violates their personal human rights – it also sends a stark warning to other legal professionals and human rights defenders.” They noted that such actions had a “wider chilling effect” on the legal profession in the country and undermined lawyers’ ability to represent politically sensitive or human rights cases “without fear of reprisal”. In the joint statement, the 23 organisations called on the government and relevant authorities to “immediately and unconditionally” release Imaan and Hadi and “take appropriate steps to have the convictions against them quashed”. It also called for an end to “misuse of the criminal justice system to target the two lawyers and drop any charges and cases against them arising solely from their work and defence of human rights”. Further, the organisations urged the government to review the use of the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act as well as anti-terrorism legislation against lawyers, journalists, human rights defenders, and peaceful critics and comply with Pakistan’s obligations under the ICCPR in terms of domestic laws and their enforcement. “Judicial remedies cannot be meaningful if a grant of liberty by one court is followed immediately by detention through another proceeding without sufficient credible evidence,” it further stated. The organisations expressed solidarity with Imaan and Hadi and “with all lawyers in Pakistan who continue to defend human rights and the rule of law despite the fear of reprisals”. “We call on the Pakistani authorities to respect their international obligations, uphold the independence of the legal profession and ensure that lawyers can exercise their profession and their human rights without intimidation, retaliation or improper interference,” the statement concluded.

items.title: Port regional de Kaolack : Tous les quais affichent plein
items.description: Le Port régional de Kaolack retrouve progressivement une animation qu’il n’avait plus connue depuis longtemps. En début de semaine, ses trois postes à quai opérationnels affichent complet, avec la présence simultanée de trois navires de 2.500 à 3.000 tonnes, engagés dans des opérations commerciales. Kaolack – Le port de Kaolack reprend des couleurs. Pour la première fois depuis des années, tous ses quais sont occupés. Un signe encourageant de la reprise des activités portuaires. Les navires présents déchargent des marchandises destinées au Mali. À l’issue de ces opérations, ils vont embarquer du sel à destination de plusieurs ports de la sous-région, notamment celui d’Abidjan. Ces rotations s’inscrivent dans le cadre de lignes régulières, avec des escales hebdomadaires à Kaolack. Sur les terre-pleins également, l’activité reprend. Marchandises, engins de manutention et dockers mobilisés donnent au site une véritable physionomie portuaire. Cette dynamique fait suite à plusieurs escales remarquées, notamment celle d’un navire de croisière en provenance des États-Unis, puis du bâtiment de guerre de la Marine nationale, le Fadiouth. Cette reprise ne doit toutefois pas occulter les contraintes liées à la navigation sur le Saloum. Il y a une semaine, un navire s’est échoué près de Lyndiane, à environ cinq kilomètres du port. Un incident qui rappelle l’urgence du dragage de la voie navigable, indispensable pour sécuriser la navigation et permettre l’accueil de navires de 5.000 à 7.000 tonnes. Pour Abdoulaye Sogue, responsable du Port régional de Kaolack, relevant du Port autonome de Dakar (Pad), cette opération devrait figurer parmi les priorités du programme d’investissements prévu dans le cadre de la célébration de la fête de l’Indépendance à Kaolack, en 2029. Annoncée par le Président de la République lors du Conseil des ministres du 13 octobre dernier, cette échéance représente une opportunité pour inscrire le dragage du Saloum parmi les projets structurants de la région. Au-delà de cette occupation exceptionnelle des quais, l’enjeu est économique et stratégique. Le Port régional de Kaolack ambitionne de jouer pleinement son rôle de plateforme complémentaire à celle de Dakar, en contribuant à sa décongestion et en offrant une alternative logistique aux opérateurs économiques. Sa position géographique constitue un atout pour capter davantage de trafic à destination du Mali et desservir les régions du centre et de l’est du Sénégal. « Elle confirme que le Port de Kaolack dispose d’une capacité opérationnelle et d’un potentiel de développement qui méritent d’être davantage valorisés au service de l’économie nationale et des échanges sous-régionaux », s’est réjoui Abdoulaye Sogue. Il a également salué les efforts de la nouvelle équipe portuaire et de l’armateur national Csttao. Ancien deuxième port de l’Afrique-Occidentale française (Aof), Kaolack entend renouer avec son prestige commercial. Depuis 2023, ses infrastructures portuaires sont gérées par le Port autonome de Dakar, dirigé par Doune Pathé Mbengue. Une intégration qui ouvre de nouvelles perspectives, à condition de consentir les investissements nécessaires, notamment le dragage du Saloum. Mamadou THIAM (Correspondant)

items.title: El juez rechaza imputar a Zapatero un nuevo delito de malversación por las joyas
items.description: José Luis Calama, juez instructor del caso Plus Ultra en la Audiencia Nacional, ha rechazado la petición de la Fiscalía Anticorrupción de imputar a José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero un nuevo delito de malversación por haberse quedado con unas joyas que, según la tesis del ministerio público, debía haber entregado a Patrimonio del Estado en caso de que fuesen un regalo recibido durante su etapa como presidente del Gobierno, como mantiene el exlíder del PSOE. El magistrado, que sigue cuestionando la versión del socialista de que las alhajas fuesen un obsequio y lo mantiene investigado por delito fiscal y contrabando, concluye que la “interpretación” de la fiscal Elena Lorente “es una construcción elaborada ex post , ya que al tiempo de los hechos ninguna disposición legal imponía que los regalos recibidos por altos cargos quedasen automáticamente incorporados al patrimonio de la Administración”; y, por tanto, no hacerlo no tiene que suponer una malversación.
